sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Joint sawing and sealing require an experienced crew; guidelines help estimate when to start sawing, but sawing speed, blade condition, and operator care all shape the final result. UFC 3-250-08 has additional joint sawing/sealing guidance.
sections.body: Joint sawing and sealing require an experienced crew to correctly perform associated tasks. Although improved guidelines are available for estimating when sawing can begin, speed of sawing, blade condition, and operator care combine to influence the final product. Find additional information in UFC 3-250-08, Standard Practice for Sealing Joints and Cracks in Rigid and Flexible Pavements.
key_points: Joint sawing/sealing quality depends on crew experience, sawing speed, blade condition, and operator care
See UFC 3-250-08 for additional joint sawing/sealing guidance
sections.applicability: Frames the chapter and cross-references UFC 3-250-08 for additional detail.

sections.title: Joint Design
sections.summary: Three pavement joint categories: isolation, construction, and contraction (Figure 9-1); detailed road/parking jointing guidance is in UFC 3-250-01, and airfield jointing guidance is in UFC 3-260-02 -- this UFC covers CONSTRUCTION of joints, not their design.
sections.body: There are three pavement categories: isolation, construction, and contraction (Figure 9-1). Find detailed guidance for jointing roads and parking areas in UFC 3-250-01. Refer to UFC 3-260-02 for guidance on airfield pavement jointing.
key_points: Three joint categories: isolation, construction, contraction (Figure 9-1)
Road/parking jointing design: UFC 3-250-01; airfield jointing design: UFC 3-260-02
This UFC (3-250-04) is the construction-practice document, not the jointing design procedure
sections.applicability: Introduces the three joint types and points to the correct design UFCs for road vs. airfield jointing.

sections.title: Isolation/Expansion Joints
sections.summary: Isolation/expansion joints separate intersecting pavements, isolate embedded fixtures such as pavement drains, or occur where pavement abuts buildings.
sections.body: The purpose of an isolation/expansion joint is to separate intersecting pavements, isolate embedded fixtures within the pavement such as pavement drains, or when pavements abut buildings.
key_points: Isolation/expansion joints separate intersecting pavements
Also used to isolate embedded fixtures (e.g., pavement drains) or at pavement-to-building abutments
sections.applicability: Applies wherever pavement intersects another pavement, an embedded fixture, or a building.

sections.title: Construction Joints
sections.summary: Construction joints separate abutting construction placed at different times, such as the end of a day's placement or between paving lanes.
sections.body: Construction joints separate abutting construction placed at different times, such as the end of a day's placement or between paving lanes.
key_points: Construction joints occur between placements made at different times (e.g., end-of-day, between paving lanes)
sections.applicability: Applies wherever separately-timed concrete placements abut one another.

sections.title: Contraction Joints
sections.summary: Contraction joints control the location of cracking from drying shrinkage or thermal contraction, and also reduce stress from slab curling and warping.
sections.body: Contraction joints control the location of pavement cracking caused by drying shrinkage or thermal contraction. Contraction joints also reduce stress caused by slab curling and warping.
key_points: Contraction joints control crack location from drying shrinkage/thermal contraction
Also reduce curling/warping stress
sections.applicability: The primary joint type used to pre-determine where shrinkage/thermal cracking will occur.

sections.title: Joint Layout Practices
sections.summary: Joint layout must check dowel/tie-bar conflicts, ensure joints line up across pilot lanes (via spot survey), plan only one sawcut longitudinal joint per set of lanes, and keep blockouts >1.2 m (4 ft) from joints where possible.
sections.body: Consider the following items when planning the joint layout: check the plans for any conflicts with dowel bars and tie bars; make sure joints line up across pilot lanes; spot survey several locations to make sure joints will line up; plan paving lanes such that only one longitudinal joint is sawcut; and plan blockouts and situate them more than 1.2 m (4 ft) from joints, when possible.
key_points: Check for dowel bar/tie bar conflicts with the planned joint layout
Spot-survey to confirm joints line up across pilot lanes
Plan blockouts more than 1.2 m (4 ft) from joints where possible
sections.applicability: Applies to the overall joint layout planning process before paving begins.

sections.title: Joint Layout Considerations
sections.summary: Introduces the inspection, jointed-plain-concrete geometry, and odd-shaped-panel considerations covered in the following subsections.
sections.body: The following are necessary joint layout considerations, detailed in the subsections below.
key_points: Covers inspection of dowel/tie-bar drawings, jointed plain concrete slab proportions, and odd-shaped panel reinforcement
sections.applicability: Introduces the joint-layout-consideration subsections that follow.

sections.title: Inspection
sections.summary: Inspect the project drawings for dowel bar and tie bar locations; discuss any noted problems with the engineer before paving.
sections.body: Inspect the project drawings for the location of dowel bars and tie bars. If any problems are noted, discuss these elements with the engineer before paving.
key_points: Inspect drawings for dowel/tie bar locations before paving
Raise any noted problems with the engineer before paving begins
sections.applicability: Applies to pre-paving drawing review of dowel/tie bar locations.

sections.title: Jointed Plain Concrete
sections.summary: For jointed plain concrete pavements, do not exceed a slab length-to-width ratio of 1.25.
sections.body: For jointed plain concrete pavements, do not exceed a slab length to width ratio of 1.25. Panels proportioned beyond this ratio are more prone to restraint-stress cracking between the planned joints.
key_points: Maximum slab length-to-width ratio for jointed plain concrete: 1.25
This ratio limit helps control restraint-stress-driven cracking within each panel
sections.applicability: Applies to sizing individual slab panels in jointed plain concrete pavement.

sections.title: Odd-Shaped Panels
sections.summary: Where rectangular slabs cannot be built, place embedded steel in both directions at >=0.05% ratio; this steel does not prevent cracking but minimizes crack opening (reducing debris infiltration and future spalling maintenance).
sections.body: Where rectangular-shaped slabs cannot be constructed (odd-shaped panels), embedded steel is placed in both directions at a ratio of at least 0.05 percent. The embedded steel will not prevent odd-shaped slabs from cracking but can minimize crack openings to reduce infiltration of debris and future spalling maintenance.
key_points: Odd-shaped panels: embedded steel both directions at >= 0.05% ratio
Steel does NOT prevent cracking -- it minimizes crack opening, reducing debris infiltration and spalling maintenance
sections.applicability: Applies to non-rectangular (odd-shaped) slab panels that cannot follow the standard jointing pattern.

sections.title: Factors Affecting Joint Spacing
sections.summary: Joints control thermal/shrinkage restraint stresses; spacing depends on concrete temperature/moisture gradients, temperature drop from final set, shrinkage, slab/base friction, modulus of base/subgrade reaction, and pavement thickness.
sections.body: The primary function of all joints is crack control. Plain concrete pavement joints are spaced to reduce thermal and shrinkage restraint stresses such that no uncontrolled cracking occurs between joints. The restraint stress magnitude influencing joint spacing depends on: concrete temperature and moisture gradients (top and bottom of slab); concrete temperature drop (relative to temperature at concrete final set); concrete shrinkage; slab/base interface friction; modulus of base/subgrade reaction; and pavement thickness.
key_points: Joint spacing controls thermal/shrinkage restraint stress to prevent uncontrolled cracking between joints
Governing factors: temperature/moisture gradients, temperature drop from final set, shrinkage, slab/base friction, subgrade modulus, thickness
sections.applicability: Establishes the physical factors behind the maximum joint spacing table (Table 9-1).

sections.title: Concrete Properties Affecting Joint Spacing
sections.summary: Key restraint-stress-driving properties: modulus of elasticity (24,000-38,000 MPa/3.5-5.5M psi, 27,000 MPa/4.0M psi typical design), coefficient of contraction (9.0-11.8x10^-6 mm/mm/C), shrinkage coefficient (250-350x10^-6 in./in.), and density (690-730 kg/m2/142-150 lb/ft2 for air-entrained concrete). Table 9-1 lists the resulting maximum joint spacing.
sections.body: Concrete properties affecting restraint stress magnitudes are: modulus of elasticity (generally 24,000 to 38,000 MPa [3.5 to 5.5 million psi]; assumed as 27,000 MPa [4.0 million psi] for most design solutions); coefficient of contraction (generally ranging from 9.0 to 11.8 x 10^-6 mm/mm/deg. C [5.0 to 6.5 x 10^-6 in./in./deg. F]); shrinkage coefficient (generally ranging from 250 to 350 x 10^-6 in./in.); and density (generally 690 to 730 kg/m2 [142 to 150 lb/ft2] for air-entrained concrete). Table 9-1 lists the maximum joint spacing: slab thickness < 9 in. (230 mm) -> 12.5-15 ft (3.8-4.6 m) spacing (10-15 ft/3.0-4.6 m for roads and parking lots); slab thickness 9-12 in. (230-305 mm) -> 15-20 ft (4.6-6 m); slab thickness > 12 in. (> 305 mm) -> 20 ft (6 m).
key_points: Modulus of elasticity: 24,000-38,000 MPa (3.5-5.5M psi); typical design value 27,000 MPa (4.0M psi)
Coefficient of contraction: 9.0-11.8e-6 mm/mm/C (5.0-6.5e-6 in./in./F)
Table 9-1 max joint spacing: <9 in. slab -> 12.5-15 ft (3.8-4.6 m); 9-12 in. -> 15-20 ft (4.6-6 m); >12 in. -> 20 ft (6 m)
Roads/parking lots use a slightly tighter spacing (10-15 ft/3.0-4.6 m) for the thinnest slab category
sections.applicability: Provides the numeric basis for selecting maximum joint spacing from slab thickness.

sections.title: In-Pavement Structures
sections.summary: Introduces light-can and joint-marking considerations for in-pavement structures, covered in the following subsections.
sections.body: This section addresses light cans and marking joint locations relative to in-pavement structures, covered in the following subsections.
key_points: Covers light-can restraint-stress management and joint-location marking
sections.applicability: Introduces the in-pavement structure subsections that follow.

sections.title: Light Cans
sections.summary: Light-can blockouts restrain slab movement and increase moisture/thermal restraint stress; embedded steel around them holds cracks tight but doesn't prevent them, and joints should be kept >1.2 m (4 ft) from light cans since closer proximity encourages cracks emanating from the can.
sections.body: Pavements with light cans require special attention. Blockouts used to install light cans can restrain slab movement and increase restraint stresses associated with moisture and thermal changes. Design engineers typically add embedded steel to slabs containing light cans; while the embedded steel does not prevent restraint cracking around light can blockouts, the steel holds any cracks that develop tight and reduces the potential for crack spalling. Since most slab movements occur near longitudinal and transverse joints, establish jointing patterns such that light cans are located more than 1.2 m (4 ft) from planned joints -- cracks tend to emanate from light cans if they are positioned closer than 1.2 m (4 ft) to joints.
key_points: Light can blockouts increase moisture/thermal restraint stress and can restrain slab movement
Embedded steel holds cracks tight (does not prevent them) around light-can blockouts
Keep light cans > 1.2 m (4 ft) from joints -- closer spacing invites cracks emanating from the can
sections.applicability: Applies to jointing pattern layout around in-pavement light can locations.

sections.title: Marking Joint Locations
sections.summary: Mark joint locations on the base, slab edge, or forms; use surveying instruments to transfer joint locations across paving lanes (especially on wide runways/taxiways), since small transfer deviations can skew joint alignment.
sections.body: Mark joint locations on the base, edge of the slab, or on the forms. When paving a runway or wide taxiway, it is challenging to transfer joint locations across pilot lanes. Use surveying instruments to transfer joint locations across paving lanes; small deviations in transferring joint locations across pavement can skew joint alignment. Carefully mark joint locations and construct joints at the proper locations.
key_points: Mark joint locations on the base, slab edge, or forms
Use surveying instruments to transfer joint locations across wide paving lanes -- small errors skew joint alignment
sections.applicability: Applies to accurately transferring joint locations across wide runway/taxiway paving lanes.

sections.title: Timing of Joint Sawing
sections.summary: Proper sawcutting timing is critical to joint performance; the following subsections cover timing, hardening factors, readiness, weather, aggregate type, delay risk, sawing-window opportunity, and equipment considerations.
sections.body: Proper timing of sawcutting is critical to optimize joint performance. Consider the timing, hardening, readiness, weather, aggregate, delay, opportunity, equipment, and hardness factors covered in the following subsections.
key_points: Introduces the sawcutting-timing factor subsections that follow
sections.applicability: Introduces the timing-of-sawing subsections that follow.

sections.title: Timing
sections.summary: Commence sawing as soon as the concrete hardens sufficiently to permit cutting without chipping, spalling, or tearing.
sections.body: Commence sawing as soon as the concrete hardens sufficiently to permit cutting without chipping, spalling, or tearing.
key_points: Start sawing as soon as the concrete can be cut without chipping, spalling, or tearing
sections.applicability: States the basic sawcutting-readiness criterion.

sections.title: Hardening
sections.summary: Concrete hardening rate is influenced by air/concrete temperature at placement, cement content, and mixture characteristics.
sections.body: Factors that influence the rate of concrete hardening: air and concrete temperatures during placement; cement content of mixture; and mixture characteristics.
key_points: Hardening rate factors: placement air/concrete temperature, cement content, mixture characteristics
sections.applicability: Applies to anticipating how quickly a given mixture will be ready for sawcutting.

sections.title: Readiness
sections.summary: Regardless of time of day or night, a contractor must be prepared to saw when the concrete is ready.
sections.body: Regardless of the time of day or night, a contractor must be prepared to saw when concrete is ready.
key_points: Contractor must be prepared to saw at any hour once concrete is ready
sections.applicability: Applies to staffing/scheduling around the sawcutting window.

sections.title: Weather
sections.summary: In warm weather concrete is usually ready for sawing 4-12 hours after placement; in cold weather, or when mixture water is below 10 C (50 F), sawing can be delayed as long as 24 hours.
sections.body: During warm weather, concrete is usually ready for sawing between 4 to 12 hours after placement. In cold weather, or when mixture water is below 10 C (50 F), sawing can be delayed as long as 24 hours.
key_points: Warm weather sawing window: typically 4-12 hours after placement
Cold weather (or mixture water < 10 C/50 F): sawing can be delayed up to 24 hours
sections.applicability: Applies to anticipating the sawcutting window based on weather and mixture water temperature.

sections.title: Aggregate
sections.summary: Mixtures with soft, coarse aggregate (e.g., limestone) generally need less strength development before sawing than mixtures with hard, coarse aggregates.
sections.body: Generally, concrete mixtures with soft, coarse aggregate, like limestone, do not require as much strength development before sawing compared to mixtures with hard, coarse aggregates.
key_points: Soft coarse aggregate (e.g., limestone) needs less strength gain before sawing than hard coarse aggregate
sections.applicability: Applies to anticipating the sawcutting window based on coarse aggregate hardness.

sections.title: Delay
sections.summary: If sawing is delayed beyond the available window, random (uncontrolled) cracking can occur instead of controlled cracking at the planned joint locations.
sections.body: If sawing is delayed, random cracking can occur. This is why timely sawing, monitored against the factors in Sections 9-4.1 through 9-4.9, is treated as a critical scheduling priority on the paving crew.
key_points: Delayed sawing risks random (uncontrolled) cracking
Timely sawing is a critical scheduling priority, not a task that can slip without consequence
sections.applicability: States the primary consequence of missing the sawcutting window.

sections.title: Opportunity
sections.summary: Several factors can shorten the joint sawing window; if it becomes too short, random cracking can develop.
sections.body: Several factors can reduce the length of the joint sawing window. If the sawing window becomes short, random cracking can develop.
key_points: A shortened sawing window (from various contributing factors) raises random cracking risk
sections.applicability: Applies to recognizing when the sawing window is under time pressure.

sections.title: Equipment
sections.summary: When sawing, the concrete must be able to support the weight of the sawing equipment and associated personnel.
sections.body: When sawing, the concrete must support the equipment weight and associated personnel.
key_points: Concrete must be strong enough to bear sawing equipment and personnel weight before cutting begins
Equipment weight-bearing capacity is one of the practical constraints on how early sawing can start
sections.applicability: Applies to confirming concrete strength is adequate to physically support sawing equipment.

sections.title: Hardness
sections.summary: Spalling along a sawcut or aggregate tearing from the surface indicates inadequate concrete hardness for sawing.
sections.body: Spalling along a sawcut or aggregate tearing from the surface indicates inadequate concrete hardness.
key_points: Spalling or aggregate tearing at the sawcut signals the concrete was not yet hard enough to cut
sections.applicability: Provides the field diagnostic sign that sawing began too early.

sections.title: Effects from Stabilized Bases
sections.summary: Stabilized-base pavement is sensitive to sawcut timing: inadequate precautions let high slab/base friction develop, and a rapid overnight temperature drop can generate shrinkage stress exceeding tensile strength; saw ASAP and continuously under adverse conditions, and whitewash asphalt-treated base surfaces to counter summer heat that shortens sawing time.
sections.body: Concrete pavement placed on a stabilized base is sensitive to sawcut timing. Inadequate precautions allow high slab/base interface friction to develop, producing uncontrolled cracking; a rapid overnight temperature drop causes shrinkage stresses in the concrete that can exceed the tensile strength and lead to uncontrolled cracking. When adverse conditions are expected, saw as soon as possible and continue until complete. Conversely, the surface of a subbase can become hot during summer conditions, increasing the temperature gradient through the slab and significantly decreasing sawing time; for asphalt treated bases, whitewash the surface of the material to increase reflectivity.
key_points: Stabilized bases raise slab/base friction, increasing uncontrolled-cracking risk under sawcut-timing pressure
Rapid overnight temperature drop on stabilized bases can generate shrinkage stress exceeding tensile strength
Whitewash asphalt-treated base surfaces in summer to reduce heat and preserve the sawing time window
sections.applicability: Applies specifically to concrete placed on stabilized (cement- or asphalt-treated) base.

sections.title: Factors That Decrease Sawing Time
sections.summary: Factors shortening the sawing window: sudden temperature drop, high wind/low humidity, high-friction or porous bases, base-slab bonding, retarded set, filling lanes late, and delayed curing application.
sections.body: Factors that shorten the time frame available for joint sawing include: sudden temperature drop; high wind, low humidity; high friction bases; bonding between base and slab; porous base; retarded set; paving fill in lanes; and delay in curing application.
key_points: Sawing-window-shortening factors: sudden temperature drop, high wind/low humidity, high-friction/porous/bonded base, retarded set, filler-lane paving, delayed curing
sections.applicability: Serves as a checklist of conditions that compress the joint-sawing window.

sections.title: Determining When to Saw
sections.summary: Sawing must occur before the concrete cracks on its own but after achieving sufficient strength to cut aggregate cleanly; the following subsections cover saw-equipment observation and temperature-based rules of thumb.
sections.body: It is difficult to determine when to saw. Sawing must occur before the concrete cracks on its own but after achieving sufficient strength to allow the saw to cut aggregate without dislodging it.
key_points: Sawing window: after enough strength to cut cleanly, before the concrete cracks on its own
sections.applicability: Introduces the saw-equipment and temperature-based timing subsections that follow.

sections.title: Saw Equipment
sections.summary: The earliest sawing time is usually determined by the equipment operator's scratch test or by observing raveling/spalling during the initial saw cut.
sections.body: Determining the earliest time to cut joints is usually based on the equipment operator's scratch test or observation of the raveling or spalling while making the initial saw cut.
key_points: Earliest sawing time is typically judged via an operator scratch test or observed raveling/spalling during the initial cut
sections.applicability: Provides the practical field method for judging earliest sawing readiness.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.summary: As a rule of thumb, sawing is limited to before the surface concrete temperature significantly decreases; once surface temperature drops and a thermal gradient forms, thermal curling restraint stresses begin, which can crack the concrete once they exceed tensile strength.
sections.body: As a rule of thumb, the limit of sawing is to cut before the surface concrete temperature significantly decreases. Under most paving conditions, the top surface temperature starts to decrease while sub-surface concrete temperatures continue to increase; once the concrete surface temperature decreases and a thermal gradient is generated, thermal curling restraint stresses start to develop, and concrete cracking results if the restraint stresses exceed the concrete tensile strength. If saw cuts are installed before significant surface cooling, curling restraint stresses remain low and cracking develops only at planned joint locations. Use surface thermometers or infrared guns to monitor concrete surface temperatures; on larger projects, monitor slab surface temperature decreases to establish guidelines for allowable surface temperature changes -- for example, if no slab cracking results in sections with a 5-degree drop in surface temperature, establish the last limit guideline for saw cutting at a 5-degree temperature drop, following that guideline until weather conditions change or other data warrant new limits. The factor of safety is reduced as the maximum allowable temperature decrease increases.
key_points: Rule of thumb: saw before the surface concrete temperature significantly decreases
Thermal curling restraint stresses build once surface cooling creates a thermal gradient -- cracking occurs if they exceed tensile strength
Sawing before significant surface cooling keeps curling stresses low so cracking stays at planned joints
Establish and follow a project-specific allowable-temperature-drop guideline (e.g., 5 degrees) using surface thermometers/infrared guns
sections.applicability: Applies to setting a temperature-drop-based sawcutting deadline for a given project.

sections.title: Maturity Meter
sections.summary: The maturity method (temperature+time via thermocouples inserted ~50 mm/2 in. deep, logged every 15-30 min) improves on temperature-only rules by accounting for both effects on strength gain, correlating with acceptable raveling/visual rating for sawcutting timing.
sections.body: An improved method to establish the early limit window of opportunity uses a concrete maturity meter. The maturity method accounts for the combined effects of temperature and time on concrete strength development. Concrete maturity meters use thermocouples installed in plastic concrete and automatically record temperatures at given time intervals; accounting for both curing temperature and time assumes a given concrete mix has the same strength at equal maturities independent of curing time/temperature histories. Thermocouples are typically inserted approximately 50 mm (2 in.) deep, as soon as possible after finishing operations; set maturity meters to acquire temperatures at 15- to 30-minute intervals. The meters automatically calculate maturity; early-age strength development is a function of ambient conditions, initial concrete temperatures, cement type, cement quantity, coarse aggregate type, and water-cementitious ratio. Maturity values can also establish early sawcutting times correlated with acceptable amounts of raveling or visual ratings.
key_points: Maturity method accounts for combined temperature-and-time effects on strength gain (vs. temperature alone)
Thermocouples inserted ~50 mm (2 in.) deep, logged every 15-30 minutes
Maturity values can be correlated with acceptable raveling/visual rating to set sawcutting time
sections.applicability: Applies as a more rigorous, instrumented alternative to temperature-drop rules of thumb for sawcutting timing.

sections.title: Joint Sawing Operation
sections.summary: A two-step sawing process: an initial cut relieves restraint stress and starts cracking at planned locations, then a second (reservoir) cut is made after hydration is complete to hold the sealant.
sections.body: A two-step process is typical for sawing joints. In the first step, the initial cut relieves restraint stresses and allows cracking to develop at planned locations. A second cut forms the sealant reservoir after the hydration process is complete.
key_points: Step 1 (initial cut): relieves restraint stress, initiates cracking at planned joint locations
Step 2 (reservoir cut): formed after hydration is complete, to hold the joint sealant
sections.applicability: Establishes the two-step sawing sequence detailed in the following subsections.

sections.title: Initial Saw Cutting
sections.summary: The first, narrow (~3 mm/1/8 in.) cut is made full-depth in one pass during rising temperatures, but during falling temperatures may need a two-pass approach (half-depth then full-depth) to avoid pop-off cracking ahead of the saw; joints are cut in placement sequence, with skip sawing (every other/third joint) an option that risks variable width and excessive sealant stress in early-cut joints.
sections.body: Items to be considered for the initial sawcut: make the first sawcut (early sawcut) with a single narrow blade (approximately 3 mm [1/8 in.] in width); perform early sawcuts made during rising concrete temperatures to the full design sawcut depth in one pass; early cuts made during falling concrete temperatures require special attention as concrete shrinkage occurs with falling temperatures -- cuts to full design sawcut depth during falling temperatures may cause random cracking (pop-off cracking) ahead of the saw, which can potentially be avoided by cutting to one-half the design depth first, followed by a second pass to design depth (discontinue sawing in any joint where a crack develops ahead of the sawcut); saw transverse joints consecutively in the same sequence as the concrete is placed in the lane. Skip sawing (cutting every other or every third joint) is sometimes used to control cracking, but can result in variable joint width and excessive sealant stresses in those joints initially sawed. Before sawing each joint, examine the concrete closely for cracks; do not saw planned joints if a crack appears near the planned joint.
key_points: Initial cut: narrow blade (~3 mm/1/8 in.); full design depth in one pass during RISING temperatures
During FALLING temperatures, use a two-pass approach (half-depth then full-depth) to avoid pop-off cracking ahead of the saw
Discontinue sawing a joint immediately if a crack develops ahead of the saw
Skip sawing (every other/third joint) risks variable joint width and excessive sealant stress in early-cut joints
sections.applicability: Applies to executing the initial (crack-relief) sawcut, including handling falling-temperature conditions.

sections.title: Reservoir Cutting
sections.summary: A wide-blade second cut forms the sealant reservoir; gang blades are prohibited (insufficient stability, spalling risk); it can be made any time before sealant installation, though later cutting improves joint face condition, and depth/width must meet the sealant's shape factor (width-to-depth ratio) requirement; monitor blade wear.
sections.body: The following considerations are for the reservoir cut: a second sawcut accommodates joint sealing material (reservoir cut), with a wide blade making the second cut to the required depth; do not use gang blades to make the second cut, since the gang blade system stability is insufficient to minimize spalling potential of the joint; the second sawcut (single or two passes) is made at any time before sealant installation, though the later in the concrete age the reservoir is formed, the better the joint face condition; assure the depth and width of the second sawcut meets the sealant's shape factor (width-to-depth ratio) requirements, since satisfactory sealant performance depends on this shape factor; and during both cuts, periodically check sawcut depth, since blades tend to wear and ride up on hard aggregates -- periodically measure blade diameter to monitor wear.
key_points: Reservoir cut: wide blade, to required depth; gang blades are PROHIBITED (insufficient stability, spalling risk)
Can be cut any time before sealant installation; later cutting gives better joint face condition
Depth/width must satisfy the sealant's shape factor (width-to-depth ratio) requirement
Periodically measure blade diameter to monitor wear (blades ride up on hard aggregates)
sections.applicability: Applies to executing the second (reservoir) sawcut that receives the joint sealant.

sections.title: Shape Factor
sections.summary: The joint sealant shape factor is reservoir width divided by depth (W/D), with its target value depending primarily on sealant type (hot-poured, silicone, two-component cold pour, or preformed compression seals).
sections.body: The joint sealant shape factor is based on the width of the reservoir divided by the depth (W/D). The value of this factor is based primarily on the type of sealant, such as hot-poured, silicone and two-component cold pour, and preformed compression seals.
key_points: Shape factor = reservoir width / depth (W/D)
Target shape factor depends on sealant type: hot-poured, silicone/two-component cold pour, or preformed compression seal
sections.applicability: Defines the shape-factor concept governing reservoir sizing for a given sealant type.

sections.title: Cleaning the Saw Cuts
sections.summary: Wet sawing leaves slurry; flush the first cut with low-pressure water then air, and reapply curing compound; the reservoir cut uses the same process at higher pressures, with curing compound unnecessary if the concrete is already sufficiently cured.
sections.body: Wet sawing leaves a slurry on the surface of the concrete and on the joint face. For the first cut, flush the slurry with low-pressure water followed by low-pressure air blasting; once the slurry is removed, reapply the curing compound along the joint. For the reservoir cut, follow the same process except increase the air and water pressures, since the concrete is hard and curing compound is not required if sufficient curing has occurred.
key_points: First cut: flush with low-pressure water then air, then reapply curing compound along the joint
Reservoir cut: same process at higher pressures; curing compound unnecessary once curing is sufficient
sections.applicability: Applies to cleaning both the initial and reservoir sawcuts after wet sawing.

sections.title: Sawcutting Equipment
sections.summary: Longitudinal contraction joints use walk-behind or early-age entry saws; transverse contraction joints use spansaws, conventional walk-behind saws, or early entry saws (no water, generally earliest cutting, max depth 100 mm/4 in. limiting use to <=400 mm/16 in. thick pavement on aggregate base); other items cover extending sawcuts through slipformed edges, restraint-cracking risk factors, and skip sawing/beveling as fallback techniques.
sections.body: Sawcutting involves several types of equipment. Longitudinal contraction joints are installed with walk-behind saws or early age entry saws. Transverse contraction joints use spansaws, conventional walk-behind saws, or early entry saws; early entry saws do not use water, are generally capable of sawing at earlier ages than spansaws or walk-behind saws, and depending on paving conditions and early-age strength gain, early-age entry sawcutting is generally possible before any surface cooling and restraint stress development -- since sawcuts are performed earlier, minimum depth requirements for the initial cut may be less; current maximum depths for early entry saws are 100 mm (4 in.), which can limit their use to pavements less than 400 mm (16 in.) thick on aggregate base. Other items: both longitudinal and transverse joints are cut at about the same time; when concrete is slipformed, extend transverse sawcuts completely through the longitudinal edge (a sawcut stopped short of the edge is shallower there, raising the risk of random cracks at outside corners; with metal pavement forms, saws must get as close to the forms as possible); the risk of early-age restraint cracking before sawcuts are installed increases if strength gain is retarded or surface temperature drops rapidly (e.g., rainfall); if sawcuts cannot be installed quickly enough, consider skip sawing (installing every third or every other transverse joint, which can lead to variable crack widths -- place roofing felt or geotextile over cracks that open significantly before placing an abutting lane; only use skip sawing when there are no other options, and consider adjusting the mixture or paving procedure first); and joint reservoir beveling (chamfering) at transverse joints increases the corner angle from 90 to about 120 degrees, reducing snow-removal-equipment damage potential at a cost increase -- if beveling is used, calculate the shape factor based on the depth of sealant where the joint face is vertical.
key_points: Early entry saws: no water, earliest cutting capability, max depth 100 mm (4 in.) -- limits use to pavements < 400 mm (16 in.) thick on aggregate base
Slipformed transverse sawcuts must extend completely through the longitudinal edge to avoid shallow-corner random cracking
Skip sawing (every other/third transverse joint) is a last-resort fallback risking variable crack widths
Reservoir beveling (90 -> ~120 degree corner) reduces snow-plow damage but increases cost; recompute shape factor at the vertical joint face
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting sawcutting equipment type and executing the sawcutting sequence, including fallback techniques.

sections.title: Joint Cleaning Before Sealing
sections.summary: Clean joints thoroughly (laitance, curing compound, foreign material) immediately before sealing via sandblasting/wire brushing/water blasting (sandblasting/wire brushing preferred, with careful nozzle technique), then oil-free air blasting as the final step; repeat air blasting for joints left open overnight/longer.
sections.body: Joint reservoir cleaning before joint sealing ensures long-term service of the sealant. Essential items: immediately before sealing, thoroughly clean joints of all laitance, curing compound, and other foreign material; use sandblasting, wire brushing, water blasting, or some combination (sandblasting or wire brushing is preferred; prime joint faces immediately after cleaning; perform sandblasting with great care because of the risk of sand particles filling the joint, applying it only to the joint face where sealant will adhere, holding the nozzle at an angle to prevent sand penetrating deeper into the joint); air blasting is the final cleaning step, with an oil-free air stream (many compressors auto-inject oil to lubricate air tools -- disconnect this line and install an effective oil/moisture trap for joint cleaning, and use new hoses since the inside of a lubricating compressor's hose is typically oil-coated; hold the nozzle no more than 50 mm [2 in.] from the pavement surface to blow debris ahead of the nozzle); and once air blasting is complete, backer rod installation and sealant application can proceed, repeating air blasting at joints remaining open overnight or for extended periods.
key_points: Sandblasting or wire brushing is the preferred cleaning method; prime joint faces immediately after
Air blasting is the final step and MUST be oil-free -- disconnect auto-oiler lines and use new hoses
Hold the air nozzle no more than 50 mm (2 in.) from the surface to blow debris ahead of it
Repeat air blasting for joints left open overnight or for extended periods
sections.applicability: Applies to the joint cleaning sequence immediately preceding sealant installation.

sections.title: Joint Sealing Issues
sections.summary: Critical joint-sealing issues span reservoir-widening timing, beveling, cleaning, sealant depth, and sealing timing; sealants must resist repeated extension/compression, jet-fuel-resistant sealants are needed near fuel spillage, and it's generally better to wait as long as possible to seal (using temporary fillers to block debris in the meantime).
sections.body: Critical issues regarding joint sealing for pavement include timing of reservoir widening, beveling, joint cleaning, depth of sealant, and timing of sealing. Other considerations: joint sealants keep out damaging material and minimize water infiltration; sealants must withstand repeated extension/compression as slabs expand/contract with temperature/moisture changes; sealant cross-section size/shape affects performance; jet-fuel-resistant sealants are necessary in refueling locations and any airfield area subject to fuel spillage; sealing timing may vary (as soon as possible, prior to placing the adjacent lane, when the pavement achieves minimum flexural strength for construction traffic, or prior to grooving operations); overall it is better to wait as long as possible to seal, since hard debris infiltrating a green cut causes spalling, and the benefits of waiting can outweigh debris-intrusion disadvantages -- use a temporary filler (backer rod or rope) to prevent construction debris infiltration in the meantime; and clean joints are necessary for all sealant materials to perform properly.
key_points: Jet-fuel-resistant sealants are required in refueling areas and anywhere subject to fuel spillage
Generally better to wait as long as possible to seal -- use temporary backer rod/rope filler to block debris meanwhile
Debris infiltrating a 'green' (freshly cut) joint before sealing causes spalling
Clean joints are essential for all sealant types to perform properly
sections.applicability: Frames the general joint sealing issues elaborated in the hot-poured/cold-poured/preformed subsections that follow.

sections.title: Hot-Poured Joint Sealing Material
sections.summary: Hot-poured sealants (asphalt/coal-tar/rubber blends) require: proper backer rod depth/shape factor with no bonding to concrete or sealant, ~25% backer rod compression, indirect-heating agitated kettles, a re-circulation-fitted application wand, bottom-to-top reservoir filling with no entrapped air, a trial installation, and recessed surface finish for early-traffic protection.
sections.body: Hot-poured sealants usually consist of some combination of asphalt, coal-tar, and rubber. Before sealing joints, the contractor must demonstrate that the equipment and procedures for preparing and placing the sealant will produce a satisfactory joint seal; the sealant must bond to the concrete surface of the joint walls, have no voids, and be tack-free after a specified time period. Key items: install closed-cell backer rod to the appropriate depth to achieve the right shape factor; the backer rod should not bond to the concrete or sealant (bonding induces stress into the seal); the backer rod must be compressed about 25 percent to maintain its position in the joint; the heating kettle should be indirect-heating type (direct heating elements can alter material properties) and needs agitators to prevent localized overheating (overheated material loses plasticity and must be discarded); fit the application wand with a re-circulation line, otherwise sealant in the hose can drop below application temperature; fill the reservoir from bottom to top, applying the sealer so the material is solid with no entrapped air; conduct a trial installation to verify the sealant can achieve a good bond; and the sealant must be recessed from the surface for protection from early traffic.
key_points: Backer rod must NOT bond to concrete or sealant, and must be compressed ~25% to hold position
Heating kettle: indirect-heating type with agitators, to prevent localized overheating (discard overheated, plasticity-lost material)
Fill the reservoir bottom-to-top with no entrapped air; conduct a trial installation first
Sealant must finish recessed from the surface for protection from early traffic
sections.applicability: Applies to installing hot-poured (asphalt/coal-tar/rubber) joint sealant.

sections.title: Cold-Poured Joint Sealing Material
sections.summary: Cold-poured sealants (polysulfides/polyurethanes/silicones, single- or two-component) require demonstrated equipment/procedures; silicone-aggregate incompatibility and moisture (both aggregate surface and reservoir) can compromise bond, requiring dry reservoirs, possible primer use, and post-cure tooling for non-self-leveling sealants.
sections.body: Cold-poured sealants are usually polysulfides, polyurethanes, or silicones -- either single-component ready-to-use, or two-component requiring onsite mixing. Before sealing, the contractor should demonstrate that equipment/procedures for preparing, mixing, and placing will produce a satisfactory installation; the sealant must bond to the joint walls, have no voids, and be tack-free after a specified time. Key items: depending on the material and manufacturer recommendation, cold-poured materials may be mixed in a paddle wheel/other mixer or fed from separate containers to a mixing nozzle that injects into the joint; silicone is self-leveling or non-self-leveling and cures by chemical reaction, liquid to solid; check for incompatibility between silicone seals and concrete aggregates, since a silicone that does not bond properly with aggregates will fail; aggregate surface moisture at sealing time can affect the silicone-concrete bond -- consider a manufacturer-provided joint primer; cold-poured materials are generally more moisture-sensitive in the reservoir, so ensure reservoirs are dry when installing sealant; cold-applied compounds are pressure-equipment-applied, forcing material to the bottom of the joint and completely filling it without spilling onto the surface; and non-self-leveling sealants require additional tooling to maintain the required depth, employed before the material cures.
key_points: Check silicone-aggregate compatibility -- poor bonding to certain aggregates causes sealant failure
Reservoir must be DRY for cold-poured materials, which are more moisture-sensitive than hot-poured
Consider a manufacturer joint primer if aggregate surface moisture threatens the silicone-concrete bond
Non-self-leveling sealants need tooling to maintain depth, applied before the material cures
sections.applicability: Applies to installing cold-poured (polysulfide/polyurethane/silicone) joint sealant.

sections.title: Preformed Joint Sealer
sections.summary: Preformed seals (extruded neoprene compression seals) are pre-compressed and inserted based on anticipated joint movement; sealant is always in compression in service, must be inserted without excessive stretch (max 2%, checked by length comparison or a pre-marked roll), lubricated, straight, vertical, and undamaged.
sections.body: Most preformed seals are made of extruded neoprene rubber, also called compression seals; the neoprene material is compressed and inserted into the joint reservoir, with pre-compression amount based on anticipated joint movement over the sealant's service life. Key aspects: the sealant must be maintained in the reservoir at a minimum amount of compression (it is always in compression); follow the sealant manufacturer's recommendations for sizing and installation; insert the sealant using a device that uniformly compresses it with nominal stretch; the sealant must be lubricated, straight, vertical, and not damaged; the installation device should not stretch the sealant, since stretching reduces allowable compression and can cause sealant failure -- maximum stretch is 2 percent; and two ways to check for stretching: (1) insert the sealant in a known length of joint, then remove and measure the extracted length; or (2) pre-measure a length of sealant with a permanent mark on the roll, then measure the installed length after installation.
key_points: Preformed (neoprene compression) seals are always in compression during service
Maximum allowable installation stretch: 2 percent
Two stretch-check methods: known-length insert-and-remeasure, or pre-marked-roll length comparison
Sealant must be lubricated, straight, vertical, and undamaged during installation
sections.applicability: Applies to installing preformed neoprene compression joint seals.

sections.title: Troubleshooting Guide
sections.summary: Early-age cracking problems are covered in Appendix D; Table 9-2 covers the non-cracking troubleshooting guide for joint sawing and sealing (poured-sealant adhesion/cohesive failure, loose preformed sealant, and raveling/spalling of the joint face).
sections.body: Early age cracking problems are discussed in Appendix D. These problems may be due to a single cause or a combination of causes. The troubleshooting guide in Table 9-2 discusses the non-cracking problems associated with joint sawing and sealing.
key_points: Early-age cracking troubleshooting is covered separately in Appendix D
Table 9-2 covers non-cracking joint sawing/sealing problems: poured sealant adhesion/cohesive failure, loose preformed sealant, raveling/spalling of the joint face
tables: Table 9-2: Troubleshooting Guide for Joint Sawing and Sealing
sections.applicability: Serves as the chapter's consolidated diagnostic reference for non-cracking joint sawing/sealing problems, cross-referencing Appendix D for cracking.
